newsitem.title: UK: West cracks whip over East European reform.
newsitem.headline: West cracks whip over East European reform.

text.p: After six years of gently nurturing the infant democracies of Eastern Europe, the West has started to crack the whip.

Top officials and bankers gathered at the annual meeting of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) have cautioned that some former communist states are straying from the path of reform and that none can rest on their laurels.

"Even though it is now increasingly unlikely that a command economy could be reimposed in the region, there is no room for complacency," President Jacques de Larosiere told the bank's annual meeting in London.
In what was cleary a concerted campaign, speakers called for tougher action to combat crime and corruption, which they said could hamper investment.

"The time has come for those who are lagging behind to pull ahead with wider and deeper reforms, so as to share in the economic revival that the best reformers are currently experiencing," Italian Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said.
There have also been persistent calls for countries to improve corporate governance and market regulation, addressing constant complaints from investors in much of the region.
Bank first vice president Ron Freeman said on Sunday that the Czech Republic, once the Western investors' favourite, had failed to combat financial fraud vigorously enough.
"Clearly there is an opportunity for the Czech Republic to regulate a bit more carefuly the financial sector so that people are better protected from fraud and misrepresentation," he said.

But Czech finance ministry director general Pavel Stepanek told Reuters Prague's reforms were on track. "Any observations that some people might have made about the Czech Republic not progressing that fast are not correcct," he said.
The EBRD was set up in 1991 to help former communist East European economies in the transition to markets.

Economic progress has varied widely. The Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland have joined the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) grouping rich industrial states and are leading candidates to join the European Union.
The bank has since shifted its focus towards Russia and former Soviet republics where reform is at an early stage.
Some East Europeans, such as the Czechs, have called for the bank to become more of a traditional commercial lender.

But de Larosiere said no country was yet ready to go without EBRD help. "There is still a high overall demand for EBRD services in advanced countries and, whilst the pattern of this demand may change, the overall level is not expected to decline in the near future," he said.
In the future, countries may be able to do without EBRD schemes -- so-called graduation, he said, adding, "Graduation is not imminent for any country."
Russian first deputy finance minister Andrei Vavilov said the EBRD had to change in line with developments in the region. "It must give more credit and have longer-term projects."
Polish central bank president Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz welcomed de Larosiere's statement saying graduation was "like a punishment for becoming a good pupil".
"Before us there is still a transformation path because we did a lot but there is a lot to do," she told Reuters, adding Poland wanted the EBRD as an investor and an equity partner.
She also said there was a lack of trained managers in Poland and added, "Our corporate governance should be more efficient."
Gronkiewicz-Walz also saw no possibility of complacency in Poland, with 4,000 enterprises still to be privatised and industries such as steel and shipbuilding to be restructured.
"Until the end of this century, it won't happen that we say 'thanks, that's enough, we are happy'."
